Issued at 417 AM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

An initial upper level wave with a plume of monsoonal moisture
will continue to lift across the area this morning bringing a
broad area of showers and thunderstorms. Just enough instability
and shear will provide for a few stronger thunderstorms,
although the more severe weather looks to be confined closer to
the low level jet in South Dakota. A lack of steep mid level
lapse rates should also diminish the hail threat, while DCAPE
values look somewhat on the low side for a wind threat this
morning. Even so, there is some diminishing of the cap in the
mix layer and storms that can develop in this area of diminished
cap may access enough shear to produce a very isolated severe 
storm this morning. Of concern are localized heavy rainfall 
this morning as pwat values of an inch to 1.5 inches are 
observed. Storm motion is also a bit on the slow side this 
morning, giving storms some longer residence time. WPC currently
has an excessive rainfall discussion for much of western and 
central ND to account for localized 1 to 3 inch rain amounts 
this morning. In fact, Hettinger reported over 2 inches when a 
heavier slow moving thunderstorm moved through overnight. These 
heavy rains could lead to some localized flooding and will have 
to be monitored through the morning. Lastly, areas without rain 
and any clearing could see patchy fog this morning as dewpoint 
values remain high and winds remain light. The rest of today, 
upper wave gets diffused as it moves east perhaps bringing a 
brief break to precipitation later this morning. Muggy 
conditions will remain with dewpoints in the 60s to lower 70s 
and highs in the mid 70s to mid 80s. SPC has maintained a 
Marginal Risk for severe weather this afternoon through this 
evening. Setup remains similar with a weak warm front left 
across the state after this mornings convection. A stacked lower
pressure system moving across southern Canada will bring a cold
front from west to east later today through this evening, while
a surface low moves just to our south across SD. The result 
could bring a period of isolated to perhaps scattered severe 
thunderstorms. Shear values may only be modest today, yet CAPE 
remains around 2000 J/KG. Favorable jet location and higher 
dewpoints may also help sustain strong storms today. There is a 
brief window the shear vectors favor discrete cells this 
afternoon. This could lead to hail to golf ball size, and winds 
to 60 MPH. This window is also where the conditional tornado 
threat sets either along the mentioned warm front or near a 
triple point near the surface low. LCLs could be lower today too
given the higher dewpoints. However, shear vector switches 
parallel quickly along the front, changing storm mode to linear 
quickly as well. STP values also are not forecast as high as 
recent days, yet could still approach 1. Overall a low tornado 
threat remains, and will keep messaging this conditional risk. 
Once storms go linear a wind threat from higher DCAPE and 0 to 3
KM shear values will be found. Winds up to 70 mph with perhaps 
some large hail with embedded supercells will be the main 
threats this evening. Pwat values of over an inch will linger 
through this evening as well. This could lead to some localized 
heavy rain again, although storm motion might be a touch 
increased by this evening given the cold front push. Even so 
HREF max ensemble QPF forecasts still showing 1 to 3 inches of 
rain still possible with these storms later today. Areas with 
heavy rain this morning followed by heavy rain later today will 
be the areas to monitor for localized flooding today. The 
eventual line of severe thunderstorms should push eastward by 
late this evening. Dry air behind this front looks to clear 
skies quickly tonight. A steady west wind should limit the fog 
potential tonight, although areas with higher rainfall amounts 
could see patchy fog. Cooler lows tonight in the mid 40s to mid 
50s can also be expected.

Monday, post frontal conditions could bring strong winds and 
fire weather concerns for much of North Dakota. The surface low
and upper low are forecast to become more vertically stacked 
over Saskatchewan, and a tight pressure gradient is expected 
across southern Saskatchewan/Manitoba into much of North Dakota.
Mostly clear skies should allow for deep mixing across these 
areas, and uniform flow in the boundary layer should allow for 
efficient mixing of stout winds to the surface. Model guidance 
suggests 850 mb winds could be in the neighborhood of 45 to 50 
knots, mainly across northern North Dakota. Should these winds 
mix down to the surface, it's possible some locations along and 
north of US-2 could experience 45 to 55 mph wind gusts during 
the day on Monday. It's possible a wind advisory may be needed 
for these areas late Monday morning into Monday afternoon.
